reason: Rich multi-source documentation establishes Deimos's discovery, physical metrics, 13 mph escape velocity, and opposing orbital destiny to Phobos.
story: In August 1877, astronomer Asaph Hall was ready to give up his search for Martian moons. His wife, Angeline Stickney, urged him to persist with the US Naval Observatory's 26-inch refractor. Within days, Hall discovered Deimos and Phobos, named after mythological twins of dread and terror. Deimos is a tiny, non-spherical world with a mean radius of only 6.2 kilometers, covered in a smooth blanket of porous regolith. Because of its minuscule mass, its surface gravity is so slight that escape velocity is just 5.6 meters per second, or about 13 miles per hour. A human sprinting fast enough could launch straight off Deimos into Mars orbit. Today, the two sibling moons face opposite fates: inner moon Phobos is spiraling inward toward destruction, while Deimos is slowly spiraling outward, destined to escape Mars's gravitational grip entirely.
angle: With an escape velocity of just 13 miles per hour (5.6 meters per second), a human running at a full sprint could launch themselves directly off Deimos into orbit around Mars.

claims.claim: Asaph Hall discovered the Martian moon Deimos in August 1877.
Deimos was discovered on August 12, 1877.
Hall made the discovery at the US Naval Observatory in Washington, D.C.
Hall used the observatory's 26-inch refracting telescope, then the largest in the world, to discover the moons.
Hall was on the verge of abandoning his search until his wife, Angeline Stickney, encouraged him to continue.
Hall discovered Mars's inner moon, Phobos, six days after Deimos, on August 18, 1877.
The moons were named Deimos and Phobos after the mythological sons or companions of Ares (Mars) from Homer's Iliad.
Deimos personifies terror or dread, while Phobos personifies fear or panic.
Deimos is the smaller and more distant of the two Martian satellites.
Deimos has a mean radius of approximately 6.2 kilometers (3.9 miles).
The escape velocity from the surface of Deimos is approximately 5.6 to 6 meters per second (13 miles per hour or 20 kilometers per hour).
Deimos takes approximately 30.3 hours to complete one orbit around Mars.
Deimos orbits Mars at a distance of approximately 23,460 kilometers.
Deimos has a noticeably smoother surface than Phobos because its craters are partially filled with porous regolith.
The regolith on Deimos has a radar-estimated density of approximately 1.471 grams per cubic centimeter.
Tidal forces cause Phobos to spiral inward toward Mars, while Deimos slowly spirals outward and will eventually escape Mars's gravity.
Phobos is predicted to collide with Mars or break apart into a ring within tens of millions of years.
In March 2023, the United Arab Emirates' Emirates Mars Mission conducted a close flyby and captured detailed close-up images of Deimos.
Japan's space agency (JAXA) is developing the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, planned to launch in 2026 to study both moons and return a sample.
The origin of Mars's moons remains unresolved, with leading hypotheses including captured asteroids, accretion from giant impact debris, or the disruption of a common parent body.

disputed: The exact origin of Deimos and Phobos remains disputed between capture of outer-belt asteroids, giant impact accretion, or progenitor breakup; the script should present these as competing scientific hypotheses.

The folk idea that escaping Deimos throws an object into interplanetary space is inaccurate; escaping Deimos's 5.6 m/s gravity puts an object into Mars orbit, though Deimos itself is slowly escaping Mars over eons. The script should explicitly clarify it launches into Martian orbit.

Jonathan Swift's fictional description of two Martian moons in Gulliver's Travels was claimed by Soviet designer V. G. Perminov to be deciphered Martian records, but astronomers consider it an educated guess by analogy; attribute Perminov's claim as fringe speculation or omit.
